label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
26 October 2026

Dear Kelechi,

You said if I was serious I should put it in writing. So I've put it in writing. Printed it, folded it, bought a stamp like a man from 1998. Enjoy it on the train. Try not to cry in front of the commuters.

I know you're reading this with that face you do — the one where your mouth is doing nothing but your eyebrows are saying *see this idiot*. That's fine. Read it anyway.

What I keep coming back to is what you said at my birthday. Not the part where you finished the small chops I'd been guarding. The spreadsheet part. Nine years, you said. Same spreadsheet, different tabs. Then you laughed and changed the subject, which is what you always do when you've accidentally said something true.

So I'm going to be serious for a bit. Abeg, bear with me.

You were the one who taught half of Moremi how to do maths before exams. Not a paid tutor — you, in a corridor, with a biro and the back of somebody's lecture note, at 11pm, when you could have been asleep or out. You got an A in further maths and instead of guarding it like a trophy you sat there explaining indices to people who were still shaky on fractions. And you had that thing — that thing where you explain something and the person doesn't feel stupid for not already knowing it. Some teachers never learn that in twenty years. You had it at nineteen, for free, in a hostel.

I saw it again at Christmas with my nephew. Three spoons of jollof rice on a plate. *This is the whole thing. This is half. Now what's a third?* He's nine and he still talks about it. He talks about fractions like it was a football match.

That's not a small thing. That's the entire job, really.

Here's the situation at my place. 1,100 kids in Peckham, and two Year 9 maths groups have had a supply teacher since September. Not because the school is a disaster — it isn't, I've been there since 2019 and I'd tell you if it was — but because there aren't enough of us. Real children sitting there getting whoever's free that morning. Some of those kids are lovely. Some of them are hard work, and I'll come to that.

The route I'd point you at is the salaried one. One year, in school from day one, and they pay you while you train. Actual salary, not a bursary, not "we'll see." Lower than yours — I'm not going to insult you by pretending otherwise. Starts September 2027. Applications open soon, which is not an accident, this is me nudging you while the door's still open.

Now the part you'd accuse me of leaving out.

Year one money drops. Properly drops. You'll feel it, you'll be annoyed about it, and you'll mention it roughly once a week. There's a pension and there are holidays that people in your office would commit crimes for, and the pay goes up in steps and becomes reasonable, but year one is a squeeze. I'm not dressing it up as a clever financial move.

The marking is endless. Endless is not a figure of speech here. There are evenings I'm still marking at 10pm, questioning every decision I've made since I was nineteen. Behaviour some days is pure wahala. You'll meet a Year 9 who has decided today is the day, and you'll be tired, and in that moment nothing about it will be funny. First term of my first year I sat in my car and cried. Twice. Engine off, phone face down, absolutely pathetic. I'm telling you that because if I only gave you the nice bits you'd know I was selling you something — and you're too sharp for that, and also you'd be insufferable about it for years.

It gets better, though. Not in a motivational-poster way. It gets better because you learn the job and the kids learn you, and then one day a lesson goes right and you walk out of the building feeling like a person again.

Last month, Damola in Year 11 finally got simultaneous equations. Three weeks we'd been on it. Three weeks. Then something clicked and he shouted "is that all??" loud enough to hear in the corridor, and the whole class clapped. Clapped. For algebra. You can't buy that in a cost report, my guy.

And before you start with the age thing — you're 34, not 84. A woman in my department started at 41 and she's one of the best teachers in the building. Your nine years aren't wasted either. Half of teaching is standing in front of thirty people who don't want to be there and getting them to do something they think they can't do. You've been managing difficult humans and impossible deadlines since you were 25. You're just doing it for a spreadsheet.

So here's all I'm asking. Much smaller than a career change.

Thursday 19 November, 6pm, the training partnership in Lewisham. Open evening. You come, you listen, you ask the awkward questions you were going to ask anyway, and afterwards we go and eat something and you tell me I've lost my mind. I'll meet you there or we can travel down together, whichever. Sign nothing. Bring nothing. Just come and look at it.

If after that you still want the spreadsheet, fine. I'll drop it. I'll only bring it up at Christmas and possibly your birthday.

But you said something on your last birthday that I haven't forgotten. You said you wanted to do something that mattered before you're 40. You've got six years. This letter is me taking you seriously.

And — with love — you can't spend the next ten years moaning at people's birthday parties about the same job. It's not fair on you, and it's not fair on the small chops.

Come on the 19th. If it's rubbish I'll say so. If it's good, you'll know.

Yours, still in the maths game,

[Your name]

P.S. If you're reading this on the train and somebody asks what it is, tell them it's a job offer. It's funnier.
